latin.1893: THESIS I. DURANDUS Vir inter Veteres Scholasticos celebris, censuit & docuit Deum cum causis secundis concurrere remote & mediate solum: nempe quia rebus omnibus propriam naturam & essentiam dedit, & facultatem agendi contulit, ac utramque Virtute sua continuo conservat: ea lege, ut creaturae singulae Virtute semel a Deo indita, & perpetuo conservata, proprios motus deinceps obeant; absque eo quod Deus earum actus & effectus immediate & per se attingat: Unde sequitur Deum actuum creaturae causam tantum remotam esse, solam vero creaturam causam proximam & immediatam.
latin.1894: II. Inter recentiores vero Ludovicus quidam a Dola ex ordine Capucinorum, cujus liber cum multis Doctorum approbationibus in lucem editus est, ad illam Durandi sententiam accedit. Dicit enim, Deum cum homine in agendo concurrere nihil aliud esse quam Vel liberum arbitrium creare, ut in actibus naturalibus, Vel dare in supernaturalibus potentiam, seu habitum agendi, per quam ipsa Voluntas totum faciat in omni actu supernaturali, absque ullo alio Dei concursu immediato actionem actu promovente. Prout hujus Viri Verba referuntur a Samuele Retorforti Theologiae Professore in Academia Andreapolitana Disputatione Scholastica de divina providentia cap. 25.
latin.1895: III. Porro juxta hos Doctores nulla est difficultas in conciliando divino concursu cum libertate actuum humanorum, quandoquidem Deus ad illos immediate non concurrit, sed mediate tantum per liberum arbitrium quod semel creavit & perpetuo conservat.
latin.1896: IV. Verum ista opinio communiter in Schola Romana rejicitur. Paucissimis enim exceptis, consentiunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae tum Veteres tum recentiores, Deum ita cooperari causis secundis ut nulla sit actio causae secundae quae proxime non procedat a Deo sicut & a causa secunda, & nullam actionem posse a creatura exerceri, nisi Deus cum creatura conferat Esse illi actioni, & quidem per se & immediate.
latin.1897: V. Illud autem colligunt ex quibusdam Scripturae locis. Praecipuus ille est qui habetur Act. 17. 28. In ipso vivimus & movemur & sumus. Quum enim dicit Apostolus nos in Deo, id est, per illum & esse & vivere, satis docet Deum esse qui & naturam & facultates omnes nobis initio dedit & jugiter conservat; adeoque quum addit nos quoque in Deo moveri, plane docere videtur omnes nostros motus atque actiones sicut naturam ipsam, immediate a Deo procedere, & Virtute illius fieri.
latin.1898: VI. Huc etiam referunt quod dicit Christus Joan. 5. 17. Pater meus usque modo operatur & ego operor. Etenim jugis illa operatio quae ibi Deo tribuitur, commodius exponi non potest quam de influxu continuo quo Deus ad omnes rerum creatarum actiones concurrit easque cum illis producit: praesertim cum manifestum sit Christum illic intelligere operationem similem ejus quam modo in sanatione claudi exercuerat.
latin.1899: VII. Idem praeterea inferri posse putant ex omnibus iis locis ubi Scriptura Deo singulariter tribuit ea quae quotidie fiunt in natura per causas secundas. Ut quum Psalm. 104. dicitur Deus rigare montes de superioribus suis, producere foenum jumentis & herbam quae homini serviat. Et Psalm. 135. Educere nubes ab extremo terrae, fulgura in viam facere, Et producere Ventos de thesauris suis. Et in Novo Testamento foenum agri circumvestire, id est, ornare floribus, Et Unicuique seminum dare proprium corpus, Matth. 6. 30. 1 Cor. 15. 38. Nec enim videtur Scriptura his & similibus modis loquendi usura fuisse, si in ejusmodi rebus nulla singularis & immediata Dei actio interveniret: nec aliam causam haberent proximam & immediatam, quam naturam ipsam a Deo creatam.
latin.1900: VIII. Illis vero Scripturae sacrae testimoniis addunt etiam argumentum a ratione naturali petitum, sic enim ratiocinantur. Nullae substantiae creatae in rerum natura permanere possunt, nisi Deus illas immediate influxu suo conservet; multo magis ergo simili influxu egent substantiarum motus & actiones: quomodo enim verum esse posset accidentia minus a Deo pendere ad sui conservationem quam ipsas substantias? Cum vero id quod ad conservationem rei est necessarium, majori cum ratione necessarium sit ad primam ejusdem rei productionem, inde consequens est ut nihil omnino a causis secundis valeat produci, nisi simul actualis immediatusque influxus causae primae interveniat.
latin.1901: IX. Ex his & similibus, communi jam fere consensu, concludunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Deum cum causis omnibus secundis, sive necessariis, sive liberis, aut contingentibus, ad singulos earum actus concurrere & cooperari, & quidem proxime & immediate. Attamen quum quaeritur quae sit illa causae primae cum causa secunda cooperatio, & qua in re consistat, magna reperitur inter Doctores Scholasticos sententiarum varietas.
latin.1902: X. Thomas & plerique illius sequaces, quales praecipue sunt Dominicani, docent ad divinum concursum explicandum, non satis esse si dicamus simpliciter, Deum influere in actus & effecta varia causarum secundarum, illisque tribuere & conservare suum esse, sicut ipsas causas secundas, & earum Virtutes creavit & conservat: Sed praeterea requiri contendunt, ut Deus ipsas causas secundas praemoveat & applicet ad opus, absque quo nihil illae prorsus acturae forent. Hoc enim exigere dependentiam causarum secundarum a Deo, ut a primo movente. Quippe ex eorum mente Deus propterea dicitur primum movens, quia ipse omnes alias causas antecedenter movet & applicat ad operationes suas, adeoque prius natura, etsi non tempore, effectus omnes causarum secundarum producit. Ut loquitur Estius in 2. Sententia ad distinct. 24. paragr. 14.
latin.1903: XI. Quae videtur esse Doctrina Catechismi ipsius Romani Tridentini Concilii jussu in lucem editi, cujus haec Verba sunt in explicatione Symboli ad primum articulum sub finem. Non solum Deus Universa quae sunt providentia sua tuetur atque administrat, Verum etiam quae moventur & agunt aliquid, intima Virtute ad motum atque actionem ita impellit; ut quamvis causarum secundarum efficientiam non impediat, praeveniat tamen: cum ejus occultissima vis ad singula pertineat, & quemadmodum sapiens testatur, Attingat a fine usque ad finem fortiter, &c.
latin.1904: XII. Igitur illi volunt Deum ciere atque applicare causam secundam ad agendum, & ratione ac natura prius quam creatura operetur, illam a Deo moveri efficaciter in singulis ejus actionibus; Deumque esse qui agit & facit ut creatura agat & faciat quicquid illa facit & agit: ita ut sine hac Dei praemotione nihil omnino possit agere creatura, & data hac praemotione impossibile sit in sensu composito, causam secundam non illud agere & facere, ad quod a prima causa praemovetur.
latin.1905: XIII. Cum vero juxta eorum sententiam, divina ista praemotio locum habeat non minus in agentibus liberis quam in necessariis, inde oritur non parva difficultas, quomodo illud cum creaturarum libertate constare possit. Si enim Voluntas nostra nihil agere potest, nisi a Deo prius moveatur, atque ad opus applicetur, quomodo censeri poterit domina sui actus, & indifferens esse ad agendum, vel non agendum; quandoquidem non habet in sua potestate divinam illam motionem & applicationem, quae ad singulos ejus actus praerequiritur? Et rursus quum Deus Voluntatem movet & applicat ad opus, qui possit dici Voluntas libere operari, cum non possit non operari, & motioni divinae resistere?
latin.1906: XIV. Bellarminus ut difficultatem illam solvat, dicit influxum, seu Virtutem Dei, qua Voluntas movetur & applicatur ad opus, recipi in causis secundis secundum illarum dispositionem. Illa vero dispositio secundum quam recipitur in Voluntate motus Dei, Bellarmino nihil aliud est quam negativa quaedam determinatio praecedens tum influxum Dei, tum actum elicitum Voluntatis. Nimirum illa ex ejus sensu, in eo consistit quod Voluntas sinat se moveri ab objecto per rationem ipsi proposito, vel ab eo se moveri non sinat. Quam determinationem dicit esse negativam, quia non consistit in actu positivo, sed in negatione actus; cum tamen Voluntas non minus sit libera ut agat, quam ut non agat. Unde fieri putat ut Voluntas sit vere libera, & ipsa se determinet, tametsi Deus illam moveat & applicet ad opus, quia, scilicet, ipsa Dei motio in ejus potestate est. Nam, inquit, si se moveri sinat ab objecto proposito, Deus eam applicat & movet ad actum eliciendum: si non sinat, Deus eam non applicat neque movet: ad hoc, scilicet, Deus se libere obligavit, quando liberam Voluntatem creavit. De Liber. Arbitr. lib. 4. cap. 16.
latin.1907: XV. Itaque ad argumentum, ex Bellarmini mente, dicendum est, quanquam Voluntas ad agendum egeat Dei motione praevia, & applicatione ad opus, illam tamen semper esse actus sui dominam; quia nimirum motionem illam quadantenus habet in sua potestate, qua ratione jam expositum est. Et quamvis posita Dei motione impossibile sit quin voluntas moveatur, voluntatem tamen semper in agendo liberam esse, quia fuit in ejus potestate a Deo non moveri; nempe se non disponendo per negativam illam determinationem ad motionem Dei recipiendam, quod erat penes voluntatem.
latin.1908: XVI. Verum ista Bellarmini solutio non placet multis eorum qui cum Thoma sentiunt, Voluntati, ut reliquis omnibus causis secundis, necessariam esse ad agendum praeviam quandam Dei motionem & applicationem. Statuunt enim Deum, absque ulla consideratione istiusmodi negativae determinationis quae in Voluntate creata praecesserit, Voluntatem pro suo arbitrio movere; neque movere simpliciter, sed ad sic, vel sic operandum efficaciter impellere: ita ut Voluntas ad hoc, & non aliud agendum, hoc volendum, illud nolendum a Deo determinetur, prius natura quam ipsa se determinet.
latin.1909: XVII. Et haec est quae ab ipsis dicitur Praedeterminatio, quam etiam Physicam appellant, non prout Physicum, id est, naturale opponitur Supernaturali, sed prout Physicum opponitur Morali. Nimirum volunt Deum Voluntates creatas ad agendum praedeterminare, non simpliciter objectum proponendo, suadendo, alliciendo, quae sunt Causae Moralis propria; sed immediate ipsam Voluntatem movendo, & actionem veram, realem & proprie dictam in eam exercendo, quod est proprium causae quae Physica vocatur.
latin.1910: XVIII. Istiusmodi vero praedeterminationem locum habere volunt non tantum in actibus bonis causarum liberarum, sed etiam in malis. Cum enim existiment eam esse causae secundae dependentiam a prima ut nihil omnino operari possit, nisi a prima moveatur, & ad agendum applicetur tanquam illius instrumentum, huic suo dogmati consentanee docent, etiam ad actus illos quibus adhaeret aliqua malitia & pravitas, Voluntatem creatam sic a Deo praemoveri & praedeterminari, ut posita Dei motione, illam hoc & illud agere necesse sit.
latin.1911: XIX. Inde tamen sequi negant Deum esse peccati authorem: quoniam Deus in actu peccati non aliud efficit quam id quod in eo est positivum, adeoque bonum; ac proinde non ad aliud movet & determinat: pravitas vero & vitiositas quae tali actui adhaeret, non est aliquid positivum, quod opus habeat causa proprie efficiente, sed solum rectitudinis debitae privatio, quae ex defectu creatae Voluntatis oritur.
latin.1912: XX. Hanc doctrinam accurate & distincte tradit Didacus Alvares in Summa Operis de Auxiliis divinae gratiae libro secundo. Etenim in eo libro capitis septimi Lemma est, Quod Deus praevia motione Voluntati creatae inhaerente eam ad modum causae Physicae moveat, applicet, seu praedeterminet ad omnes actus suos bonos in particulari, salva ipsius libertate. Et in eo capite haec sunt illius verba, Per hanc motionem & applicationem Deus transmutat realiter Voluntatem de uno in aliud, & facit illam de Nolente Volentem. Item, Deus hac actuali motione efficaci ad modum causae Physicae, id est, vere efficienter, praedeterminat hominis Voluntatem ad liberos actus bonos, ut Voluntas a Deo mota per hujusmodi auxilium se libere & infallibiliter determinet ad actum secundum libere producendum.
latin.1913: XXI. Caput vero nonum hunc titulum praefert. Quod Deus praevia motione liberum arbitrium vere efficienter, sive ad modum causae Physicae, praemoveat ad actum peccati, in quantum actus, & ut ens est. Ipsum vero caput incipit his verbis, Quae dicta sunt de praedeterminatione Voluntatis ad actus bonos, extendi debent ad actum peccati, in quantum actus & ens est. Unde quicquid entitatis reperitur in quocunque actu peccati, etiamsi alias sit intrinsece malus, debet reduci in Deum, tanquam in primam causam praemoventem, & praedeterminantem actuali motione Voluntatem creatam ad talem actum, in quantum actus est, & secundum quod est ens. Postea vero ostensurus quomodo ex eo quod Deus est causa prima praemovens, & praedeterminans voluntatem creatam ad actum intrinsece malum, exempli gratia ad actum blasphemiae, aut odii in Deum, non sequitur Deum esse causam malitiae moralis quae talibus actibus inest, dicit deformitatem peccati, seu malitiam moralem non sequi intrinsece, & ex natura rei ad actum blasphemiae, vel odii Dei, secundum suam essentiam, ut actus est; neque ut est ens in genere naturae, etiam in individuo; sed ut procedit a voluntate creata deficiente; & ideo in voluntatem deficientem, & non in Deum, debere refundi malitiam moralem, & defectum peccati.
latin.1914: XXII. Atque his consentanea sunt quae leguntur apud Estium loco supra citato, ubi exposita eadem sententia, & multis in illius confirmationem adductis, sic concludit, & adversus voluntatis humanae libertatem sibi objicit, Cum igitur ex dictis pateat voluntatem nostram ad actiones suas efficaciter moveri & determinari a Deo tanquam prima causa, primoque agente, movente, deliberante, & proinde ab eo praeveniri ac praedeterminari, restat explicandum quomodo cum efficaci illa motione, ac determinatione, imo praemotione ac praedeterminatione divina, consistat libertas voluntatis nostrae. Non enim videtur relinqui liberum ad utrumlibet id quod a priori causa efficaciter movetur & determinatur in alteram partem.
latin.1915: XXIII. Ad hoc vero respondet ad rationem liberi arbitrii; hoc sufficere, ut ex praevio judicio intellectus practici, sic eligat unum oppositorum, ut tamen ex ejusdem intellectus diverso judicio possit eligere alterum; quia, scilicet, radix & fundamentum libertatis arbitrii est in intellectu, quatenus ille diversas boni rationes circa opposita potest considerare, & voluntati proponere, rationem vero liberi arbitrii non includere, ut dum agens liberum ex judicio praevio eligit, ad sic judicandum atque eligendum non moveatur ab aliqua causa superiori. Ac proinde cum motio Dei voluntatem praedeterminans non impediat quominus homo plenum atque perfectum habeat judicium rationis, & judicet aliud medium esse contingens, aliud autem cum fine ex necessitate connexum, & posset quoque ex diverso judicio aliud eligere, hoc ipso, talem motionem libertati Voluntatis nostrae nihil officere. Quippe proprium esse Voluntatis increatae ut electionem suam ab aliquo priori non habeat.
latin.1916: XXIV. Alia tamen ratione conciliare conatur Alvares Physicam illam Voluntatis humanae praedeterminationem ad actus ipsius singulos per Dei moventis impulsum, cum libera ejusdem Voluntatis electione. Postquam enim hanc sibi objectionem proposuit, si praevius ille Dei influxus in causam est necessarius, ut Voluntas operetur, sequitur quod sine illo operari non possit, & ita peribit ejus libertas, Respondet, Praevia illa motio, sive influxus immediatus in causam, non est necessarius ut Voluntas possit operari, si velit; id enim habet per propriam Virtutem, aut per habitus supernaturales; sed solum est necessarius ut actualiter operetur. Unde ex eo quod voluntas non moveatur a Deo praevia illa motione, non sequitur quod non possit velle, aut operari; sed solum infertur quod de facto non sit operatura.
latin.1917: XXV. Ejusdem vero libri cap. 6. Responsione ad secundum argumentum, ex eo quod Deus aliquem praedeterminavit ad hoc, vel illud volendum, negat sequi quod absolute loquendo, non sit in potestate ejus aliud velle, quamvis ex suppositione divinae illius praedeterminationis, impossibile sit, in sensu composito, quod velit aliud objectum. Uno verbo distinguit inter velle & operari, & posse velle atque operari; & concedit absque influxu illo praedeterminante voluntatem nunquam operari, cum eo vero voluntatem nunquam non operari: sed pertendit, cum illo voluntatem habere potestatem non operandi, & contra absque illo voluntatem habere potestatem operandi, scilicet in sensu diviso. Nimirum ex ejus mente, cum influxu isto praedeterminante stat potentia voluntatis ad non agendum, aut aliter agendum; non stat vero actus oppositus, aut cessatio ab actu. Et vice versa, absque illo influxu manet in voluntate potentia agendi, licet absque illo nunquam in actum educatur. Inde autem colligit fieri ut omittens actum qui est in praecepto libere illum omittat, & peccet; quia per auxilium sufficiens poterat implere illud praeceptum; ex Dei autem misericordia poterat habere motionem illam ad agendum necessariam, sua vero culpa impedivit ne illi donaretur a Deo.
latin.1918: XXVI. Sed multo major pars Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae sententiam istam hodie rejicit, & pertendit influxum illum praemoventem & praedeterminantem voluntates hominum ad singulos ipsorum actus, humani arbitrii libertatem prorsus evertere; ac praeterea inde sequi Deum esse peccati authorem, ut qui, ex ista sententia, homines praedeterminet etiam ad actus intrinsece malos, & quandam male agendi necessitatem iis imponat.
latin.1919: XXVII. Itaque longe aliter de concursu illo Dei philosophantur. Primo enim statuunt, Deum cum causis secundis concurrentem & cooperantem non aliquid agere, aut imprimere in ipsam facultatem quae agit, exempli gratia, in voluntatem nostram; sed tantum immediate influere & agere in ipsam actionem, & effectum causae secundae, eamque producere illo ipso momento quo producitur a causa secunda.
latin.1920: XXVIII. Deinde consequenter docent actionem causae primae concurrentis cum causa secunda, non esse actionem reipsa diversam ab actione causae secundae, sed illam ipsam actionem, quatenus esse suum a causa prima accipit. Ita quum Deus, verbi causa, cum voluntate concurrit in volendi, vel nolendi actu, ipse non exerit, ex eorum mente, actionem aliquam in voluntatem, distinctam ab actione voluntatis ipsius; sed tantum esse confert actioni voluntatis simul cum voluntate, & actionem illam conservat. Ac proinde divina hac in parte cooperatio non est aliquid diversum a volitione nostra, sed ipsa nostra volitio, quatenus a Deo immediate pendet quoad sui productionem & conservationem.
latin.1921: XXIX. Praeterea, quod etiam manifeste sequitur ex dictis, negant causam secundam a causa prima ad agendum moveri, aut ab eadem in agendo ad talem actionem edendam determinari. Adeoque, juxta eorum sententiam, causa secunda, & proinde voluntas, non ideo operatur quia Deus illam movet, & applicat ad agendum: sed potius Deus illi cooperatur, quia ipsa sese ad agendum disponit. Concursus autem & influxus divinus est aliquid ex se indifferens, quod a causis secundis ad varias actionum species determinatur.
latin.1922: XXX. Haec & plura ejusdem generis prolixius diducta & exposita videre est apud Ludovicum Molinam in Concordia Liberi Arbitrii cum gratiae donis, &c. quaest. 14. disputat. 26. Ubi affirmat primo Deum ita cum causis secundis concurrere ad earum operationes & effectus, ut quemadmodum causa secunda immediate elicit suam operationem, & per eam terminum, seu effectum producit; sic Deus concursu quodam generali immediate influat cum ea in eandem operationem, & per operationem, seu actionem terminum illius, seu effectum producat. Secundo, Deum, quando concurrit cum causis secundis, influere ut causam universalem, influxu quodam indifferenti ad varias actiones & effectus, determinari vero influxum illum generalem ad diversas species actionum & effectuum a particulari influxu causarum secundarum, qui pro diversitate virtutis cujusque ad agendum diversus est. Non secus ac influxus solis, qui etiam universalis est, determinatur ab influxu hominis, ut producatur homo; & ab influxu equi, ut oriatur equus. Quod si causa libera sit, in ipsius potestate esse ita influere, ut producatur potius haec actio quam illa, puta velle, quam nolle, aut ambulare, quam sedere, & hic effectus potius quam ille, nempe hoc artefactum, potius quam aliud; Vel etiam suspendere omnino influxum, ne ulla sit actio. Tertio, ad nullius effectus productionem satis esse influxum Dei per concursum universalem, sine influxu causae secundae particularis a qua determinatur, neque vicissim influxum causae particularis, sine influxu Dei per concursum universalem, quo adjuvetur, & quem de lege ordinaria statuit nunquam denegare. Hos vero duos influxus mutuo ab invicem pendere, ut in rerum natura existant: imo non esse duas actiones, sed unam numero actionem, quae ut est a Deo illo modo influente, dicitur concursus generalis; ut vero a causa secunda, puta ab igne calefaciente, dicitur concursus, seu influxus ignis. Neque actionem illam habere quod sit hujus speciei, nempe calefactio, potius quam frigefactio, quia est a Deo per concursum universalem, sed quia est ab igne cum Deo cooperante per suam particularem virtutem.

sections.title: Durandus: God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. DURANDUS a Man celebrated among the Old Schoolmen, thought and taught that God concurs with second causes remotely and mediately only: namely because he gave to all things their proper nature and essence, and conferred the faculty of acting, and continually preserves both by his Power; on this condition, that each creature by the Power once put into it by God, and perpetually preserved, should thereafter perform its own motions; without God reaching their acts and effects immediately and by himself: Whence it follows that God is only the remote cause of the acts of the creature, but the creature alone the proximate and immediate cause.
pass_b: Durandus, a well-known figure among the older scholastics, held and taught that God concurs with secondary causes only remotely and mediately.

On his account God gave everything its own nature and essence, bestowed the power to act, and keeps both in being by his continual power. He did so on the understanding that each creature, by the power God once placed in it and always sustains, then carries out its own motions, without God touching its acts and effects directly and of himself. It follows that God is only the remote cause of what creatures do, and the creature alone is the proximate and immediate cause.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: Among recent writers Louis of Dole, a Capuchin, follows Durandus (as reported by Rutherford)
sections.pass_a: But among the more recent a certain Louis of Dole of the order of Capuchins, whose book was put forth with many approbations of Doctors, accedes to that opinion of Durandus. For he says, that for God to concur with man in acting is nothing else than Either to create free choice, as in natural acts, Or to give in supernatural acts a power, or habit of acting, by which the Will itself does the whole in every supernatural act, without any other immediate concurrence of God actually promoting the action. As the Words of this Man are reported by Samuel Rutherford Professor of Theology in the University of St Andrews in the Scholastic Disputation on divine providence chap. 25.
pass_b: Among more recent writers, a certain Louis of Dole, of the Capuchin order, whose book appeared with many approvals from theologians, comes over to Durandus's view.

He says that God's concurring with man in action amounts to nothing more than creating free choice, in natural acts, or, in supernatural acts, giving a power or habit of acting by which the will itself does the entire work in every supernatural act, without any further immediate concurrence of God actually advancing the action. His words are reported in this form by Samuel Rutherford, professor of theology at the University of St Andrews, in his Scholastic Disputation on Divine Providence, chapter 25.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

notes: Ludovicus a Dola is the Capuchin Louis of Dole; Samuel Retorfortis is Samuel Rutherford, whose Disputatio scholastica de divina providentia Le Blanc cites.

sections.title: On this view there is no difficulty in reconciling concurrence with freedom
sections.pass_a: Further according to these Doctors there is no difficulty in reconciling the divine concurrence with the liberty of human acts, since God does not concur to them immediately, but mediately only through the free choice which he once created and perpetually preserves.
pass_b: For these teachers, then, reconciling God's concurrence with the freedom of human acts poses no problem at all.
God does not concur in those acts immediately, but only mediately, through the free choice he created once and keeps in being without interruption.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: The Roman School commonly rejects this: God gives being to every act of the creature immediately
sections.pass_a: But that opinion is commonly rejected in the Roman School. For with very few excepted, the Doctors of the Roman Church both Old and more recent agree, that God so cooperates with second causes that there is no action of a second cause which does not proceed proximately from God as well as from the second cause, and that no action can be exercised by a creature, unless God together with the creature confer Being on that action, and that by himself and immediately.
pass_b: The Roman School, however, generally rejects this view. With very few exceptions, the teachers of the Roman Church, old and recent alike, agree that God cooperates with secondary causes in such a way that every action of a secondary cause comes proximately from God as well as from that cause.
No action can be performed by a creature unless God, together with the creature, gives that action its being, and does so of himself and directly.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: Their proof from Acts 17:28: in him we live and move and are
sections.pass_a: And this they gather from certain places of Scripture. The chief is that which is had Acts 17. 28. In him we live and move and are. For when the Apostle says that we in God, that is, through him both are and live, he sufficiently teaches that it is God who both gave us nature and all faculties at the beginning and continually preserves them; and so when he adds that we also are moved in God, he seems plainly to teach that all our motions and actions, like nature itself, proceed immediately from God, and are done by his Power.
pass_b: They draw this from certain passages of Scripture, chiefly Acts 17:28: 'In him we live and move and have our being.'

When the Apostle says that we exist and live in God, that is, through him, he makes it clear enough that God gave us our nature and all our powers at the start and constantly sustains them. And when he adds that we also move in God, he appears to teach outright that all our movements and actions, like our nature itself, come directly from God and are carried out by his power.

sections.title: John 5:17: my Father works until now
sections.pass_a: Hither also they refer what Christ says John 5. 17. My Father works until now and I work. For that continual operation which is there attributed to God, cannot be more fitly expounded than of the continual influence by which God concurs to all the actions of created things and produces them with them: especially since it is manifest that Christ there understands an operation like that which he had just exercised in the healing of the lame man.
pass_b: They also cite Christ's words in John 5:17: 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.'

The unceasing work ascribed to God there, they argue, is best explained as the continual influence by which God concurs in every action of created things and produces those actions together with them. This is all the more so because Christ clearly has in mind a work like the one he had just done in healing the lame man.

sections.title: Texts that ascribe to God what happens daily in nature
sections.pass_a: The same moreover they think can be inferred from all those places where Scripture singly attributes to God those things which are done daily in nature by second causes. As when Psalm 104. God is said to water the mountains from his upper chambers, to bring forth grass for the cattle and herb which serves man. And Psalm 135. To bring forth clouds from the end of the earth, to make lightnings into the way, And to bring forth the Winds from his treasuries. And in the New Testament to clothe the grass of the field, that is, to adorn it with flowers, And To give to each of the seeds its proper body, Matth. 6. 30. 1 Cor. 15. 38. For Scripture does not seem to have been about to use these and similar manners of speaking, if in things of that kind no singular and immediate action of God intervened: nor did they have any other proximate and immediate cause, than nature itself created by God.
pass_b: They also think the same can be inferred from every passage in which Scripture assigns to God, one by one, the things that happen daily in nature through secondary causes.

So in Psalm 104 God is said to water the mountains from his upper rooms and to make grass grow for the cattle and plants to serve mankind. In Psalm 135 he brings up clouds from the ends of the earth, makes lightning for the rain, and brings the winds out of his storehouses. In the New Testament he clothes the grass of the field, that is, decks it with flowers, and gives each kind of seed its own body (Matthew 6:30; 1 Corinthians 15:38).

Scripture would hardly have spoken this way, they argue, if no particular and immediate act of God were involved in such things and they had no proximate and immediate cause other than nature itself as God created it.

sections.title: An argument from natural reason: what preservation needs, first production needs still more
sections.pass_a: But to those testimonies of sacred Scripture they add also an argument sought from natural reason, for thus they reason. No created substances can remain in the nature of things, unless God preserve them immediately by his influence; much more therefore do the motions and actions of substances need a like influence: for how could it be true that accidents depend less on God for their preservation than substances themselves? But since that which is necessary to the preservation of a thing, is with greater reason necessary to the first production of the same thing, it is consequent thence that nothing at all can be produced by second causes, unless at the same time an actual and immediate influence of the first cause intervene.
pass_b: To these scriptural testimonies they add an argument from natural reason, which runs as follows. No created substance can continue to exist unless God keeps it in being by his immediate influence. Much more, then, do the motions and actions of substances need such influence, for how could accidents depend less on God for their preservation than substances do?

Moreover, whatever a thing needs in order to be kept in being, it needs all the more in order to be produced in the first place. It follows that secondary causes can produce nothing whatever unless an actual and immediate influence of the first cause is present at the same time.

sections.title: Hence the common Roman conclusion: God concurs proximately and immediately with every act; but how is disputed
sections.pass_a: From these and similar things, by a now almost common consent, the Doctors of the Roman Church conclude that God concurs and cooperates with all second causes, whether necessary, or free, or contingent, to each of their acts, and that proximately and immediately. And yet when it is asked what that cooperation of the first cause with the second cause is, and in what thing it consists, a great variety of opinions is found among the Scholastic Doctors.
pass_b: From these and like arguments the teachers of the Roman Church now conclude, almost unanimously, that God concurs and cooperates with every secondary cause, necessary, free or contingent, in each of its acts, and does so proximately and immediately.
But when one asks what this cooperation of the first cause with the secondary cause is and what it consists in, the scholastic teachers turn out to hold widely different views.

sections.title: Thomas and the Dominicans: God premoves and applies secondary causes to their work (Estius)
sections.pass_a: Thomas and most of his followers, such as chiefly are the Dominicans, teach that for explaining the divine concurrence, it is not enough if we say simply, that God flows into the various acts and effects of second causes, and gives and preserves to them their being, as he created and preserves the second causes themselves, and their Powers: But they contend that it is required besides, that God premove the second causes themselves and apply them to the work, without which they would do nothing at all. For this the dependence of second causes on God, as on the first mover, demands. Since according to their mind God is therefore called the first mover, because he himself antecedently moves all other causes and applies them to their operations, and so prior by nature, though not by time, produces all the effects of second causes. As Estius speaks on the 2. Sentences at distinct. 24. paragr. 14.
pass_b: Thomas and most of his followers, chiefly the Dominicans, teach that to explain God's concurrence it is not enough to say simply that God flows into the various acts and effects of secondary causes and gives them and keeps them in being, as he created and keeps in being the secondary causes themselves and their powers.

They insist that something more is needed: God must premove the secondary causes and apply them to their work, without which they would do nothing whatever. This, they say, is what the dependence of secondary causes on God as first mover requires.

On their view God is called the first mover precisely because he moves all other causes beforehand and applies them to their operations, and so produces all the effects of secondary causes first in the order of nature, though not of time. So Estius puts it on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 24, paragraph 14.

lemmas.gloss: premove and apply to the work
prior by nature, though not by time

sections.title: This seems to be the teaching of the Roman Catechism (on the first article of the Creed; Wisdom 8:1)
sections.pass_a: Which seems to be the Doctrine of the very Roman Catechism put forth by order of the Council of Trent, whose Words are these in the explanation of the Creed on the first article towards the end. God not only protects and administers by his providence All things that are, But also those which are moved and do something, he so impels by an inward Power to motion and action; that although he does not hinder the efficiency of second causes, yet he prevents it: since his most hidden force reaches to each thing, and as the wise man testifies, Reaches from end to end mightily, &c.
pass_b: This appears to be the teaching of the Roman Catechism itself, published by order of the Council of Trent. Toward the end of its explanation of the first article of the Creed it says:

'God not only protects and governs by his providence everything that exists. He also so drives the things that move and act, by an inward power, to their motion and action that, while he does not hinder the efficiency of secondary causes, he goes before it, since his most hidden power reaches to every single thing and, as the wise man testifies, "reaches mightily from one end to the other", and so on.'

sections.title: God stirs and applies the secondary cause; with the premotion given, it cannot fail to act in the composite sense
sections.pass_a: Therefore they will have it that God stirs and applies the second cause to acting, and that in reason and nature before the creature operates, it is moved efficaciously by God in each of its actions; and that it is God who acts and makes that the creature act and make whatever it makes and acts: so that without this premotion of God the creature can do nothing at all, and, this premotion being given, it is impossible in the composed sense, that the second cause not do and make that, to which it is premoved by the first cause.
pass_b: They hold, therefore, that God rouses and applies the secondary cause to act, and that before the creature works, in the order of reason and nature, God effectively moves it in each of its actions. It is God who acts and brings it about that the creature acts and does whatever it does.

Without this premotion from God the creature can do nothing at all; and once the premotion is given, it is impossible, in the composite sense, for the secondary cause not to do and make what the first cause premoves it to.

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: The difficulty: how can premotion consist with created freedom?
sections.pass_a: But since according to their opinion, that divine premotion has place no less in free agents than in necessary ones, thence arises no small difficulty, how that can consist with the liberty of creatures. For if our Will can do nothing, unless it be first moved by God, and applied to the work, how can it be thought the mistress of its act, and to be indifferent to acting, or not acting; since it does not have in its power that divine motion and application, which is prerequired to each of its acts? And again when God moves the Will and applies it to the work, how can the Will be said to operate freely, since it cannot not operate, and resist the divine motion?
pass_b: Since on their view this divine premotion applies to free agents no less than to necessary ones, a considerable difficulty arises: how can it be reconciled with the freedom of creatures?

If our will can do nothing unless God first moves it and applies it to its work, how can it be considered mistress of its own act and indifferent to acting or not acting, when the divine motion and application required beforehand for each of its acts is not in its power? And again, when God moves the will and applies it to its work, how can the will be said to act freely, when it can neither refrain from acting nor resist the divine motion?

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Bellarmine: the divine motion is received according to the will's negative determination (De Lib. Arb. IV.16)
sections.pass_a: Bellarmine to solve that difficulty, says that the influence, or Power of God, by which the Will is moved and applied to the work, is received in second causes according to their disposition. But that disposition according to which the motion of God is received in the Will, is to Bellarmine nothing else than a certain negative determination preceding both the influence of God, and the elicited act of the Will. Namely that in his sense, consists in this that the Will allows itself to be moved by the object proposed to it by reason, or does not allow itself to be moved by it. Which determination he says is negative, because it does not consist in a positive act, but in the negation of an act; since yet the Will is no less free to act, than not to act. Whence he thinks it comes about that the Will is truly free, and determines itself, although God moves it and applies it to the work, because, namely, the very motion of God is in its power. For, he says, if it allows itself to be moved by the object proposed, God applies it and moves it to eliciting the act: if it does not allow, God neither applies nor moves it: to this, namely, God freely bound himself, when he created a free Will. On Free Choice book 4. chap. 16.
pass_b: To resolve that difficulty Bellarmine says that God's influence or power, by which the will is moved and applied to its work, is received in secondary causes according to their disposition.

For Bellarmine the disposition according to which God's motion is received in the will is simply a kind of negative determination that comes before both God's influence and the will's elicited act. In his sense it consists in the will's letting itself be moved by the object that reason sets before it, or not letting itself be moved by it. He calls the determination negative because it lies not in a positive act but in the absence of one, though the will is no less free to act than not to act.

This, he thinks, is how the will is truly free and determines itself even though God moves it and applies it to its work: God's motion itself is in the will's power. 'If it lets itself be moved by the object set before it,' he says, 'God applies it and moves it to produce the act; if it does not, God neither applies it nor moves it. God freely bound himself to this when he created a free will.' (De libero arbitrio, book 4, chapter 16.)

sections.title: So, for Bellarmine, the will remains mistress of its act because the motion is in a way in its power
sections.pass_a: Therefore to the argument, according to Bellarmine's mind, it must be said, that although the Will needs for acting the previous motion of God, and application to the work, yet it is always mistress of its act; because namely it has that motion in some measure in its power, in the manner already set forth. And although, the motion of God being posited it is impossible that the will not be moved, yet the will is always free in acting, because it was in its power not to be moved by God; namely by not disposing itself through that negative determination to receiving the motion of God, which lay with the will.
pass_b: On Bellarmine's view, then, the answer to the objection is this. Although the will needs God's prior motion and application in order to act, it is always mistress of its act, because it has that motion in its power to some degree, in the way just explained.

Once God's motion is given, the will cannot fail to be moved; yet it is always free in acting, because it was in its power not to be moved by God, namely by not disposing itself, through that negative determination, to receive his motion. That was up to the will.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: Many Thomists reject Bellarmine's solution: God moves the will at his own choice, prior by nature to its self-determination
sections.pass_a: But that solution of Bellarmine does not please many of those who think with Thomas, that a certain previous motion and application of God is necessary to the Will for acting, as to all other second causes. For they lay down that God, without any consideration of such a negative determination which may have preceded in the created Will, moves the Will at his own choice; and does not move it simply, but efficaciously impels it to operating thus, or thus: so that the Will is determined by God to doing this, and not another thing, to willing this, to refusing that, prior by nature than it determines itself.
pass_b: Bellarmine's solution does not satisfy many of those who hold with Thomas that the will, like every other secondary cause, needs a certain prior motion and application from God in order to act.

They maintain that God moves the will as he chooses, without any regard to a negative determination of that kind that may have preceded in the created will. He does not merely move it but efficaciously impels it to act in this way or that, so that the will is determined by God to do this and not something else, to will this and refuse that, first in the order of nature, before it determines itself.

lemmas.latin: prius natura quam ipsa se determinet
lemmas.gloss: prior by nature than it determines itself

sections.title: This is their 'physical predetermination': physical as opposed to moral causality
sections.pass_a: And this is what is called by them Predetermination, which they also call Physical, not as Physical, that is, natural is opposed to Supernatural, but as Physical is opposed to Moral. Namely they will have it that God predetermines created Wills to acting, not simply by proposing the object, persuading, enticing, which are proper to a Moral Cause; but by immediately moving the Will itself, and exercising on it a true, real and properly so called action, which is proper to a cause which is called Physical.
pass_b: This is what they call predetermination, and they also call it physical, not in the sense in which the physical, meaning the natural, is opposed to the supernatural, but in the sense in which the physical is opposed to the moral.

They hold that God predetermines created wills to act not merely by presenting an object, urging and attracting, which is what a moral cause does, but by moving the will itself directly and exerting on it a true, real action in the proper sense, which is what belongs to a cause called physical.

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: They extend predetermination to evil acts as well as good
sections.pass_a: But they will have predetermination of this kind have place not only in the good acts of free causes, but also in the evil. For since they think that the dependence of the second cause on the first is such that it can operate nothing at all, unless it be moved by the first, and applied to acting as its instrument, consistently with this their dogma they teach, that also to those acts to which some malice and depravity adheres, the created Will is so premoved and predetermined by God, that, the motion of God being posited, it is necessary that it do this and that.
pass_b: They hold that predetermination of this kind takes place not only in the good acts of free causes but in their evil acts too.

Since they think that the secondary cause depends on the first so completely that it can do nothing unless the first moves it and applies it to act as its instrument, they teach, consistently with that doctrine, that even for acts tainted with some malice and depravity the created will is premoved and predetermined by God in such a way that, once God's motion is given, it must do this or that.

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Yet they deny God is the author of sin: he effects only what is positive; the depravity is a privation
sections.pass_a: Yet they deny that it follows thence that God is the author of sin: because God in the act of sin effects nothing else than that which is positive in it, and so good; and accordingly moves and determines to nothing else: but the depravity and viciousness which adheres to such an act, is not something positive, which needs a cause properly efficient, but only the privation of due rectitude, which arises from the defect of the created Will.
pass_b: They deny, however, that it follows that God is the author of sin. In an act of sin God brings about only what is positive in it, and therefore good, and moves and determines the will to nothing beyond that.

The depravity and corruption attached to such an act is nothing positive requiring a cause that properly produces it. It is only the absence of the rightness the act ought to have, and it arises from the failure of the created will.

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Alvarez teaches this exactly (De auxiliis II.7): God physically predetermines the will to all its good acts
sections.pass_a: This doctrine Diego Alvarez delivers accurately and distinctly in the Sum of the Work on the Helps of divine grace in the second book. For in that book the Lemma of the seventh chapter is, That God by a previous motion inhering in the created Will moves, applies, or predetermines it after the manner of a Physical cause to all its good acts in particular, its liberty being safe. And in that chapter these are his words, By this motion and application God really changes the Will from one thing to another, and makes it from Unwilling Willing. Again, God by this actual efficacious motion after the manner of a Physical cause, that is, truly efficiently, predetermines the Will of man to free good acts, that the Will moved by God through help of this kind may determine itself freely and infallibly to producing the second act freely.
pass_b: Diego Alvarez sets out this teaching accurately and clearly in the Summa of his work De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 2. The heading of chapter 7 there reads: 'That God, by a prior motion inhering in the created will, moves, applies, or predetermines it in the manner of a physical cause to all its good acts in particular, without prejudice to its freedom.'

In that chapter he writes: 'By this motion and application God really changes the will from one state to another and makes it willing instead of unwilling.' And again: 'By this actual, efficacious motion, in the manner of a physical cause, that is, truly as an efficient cause, God predetermines man's will to free good acts, so that the will, moved by God through help of this kind, determines itself freely and infallibly to produce its second act freely.'

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Alvarez II.9: God premoves free choice to the act of sin as act and being; the malice is from the deficient will
sections.pass_a: But the ninth Chapter bears this title. That God by previous motion truly efficiently, or after the manner of a Physical cause, premoves free choice to the act of sin, in so far as it is an act, and as it is a being. But the chapter itself begins with these words, What has been said of the predetermination of the Will to good acts, ought to be extended to the act of sin, in so far as it is an act and a being. Whence whatever of entity is found in any act of sin whatever, even if otherwise it be intrinsically evil, ought to be reduced to God, as to the first cause premoving, and predetermining by actual motion the created Will to such an act, in so far as it is an act, and according as it is a being. But afterwards being about to show how from this that God is the first cause premoving, and predetermining the created will to an act intrinsically evil, for example to an act of blasphemy, or of hatred against God, it does not follow that God is the cause of the moral malice which is in such acts, he says that the deformity of sin, or moral malice does not follow intrinsically, and from the nature of the thing upon the act of blasphemy, or of hatred of God, according to its essence, as it is an act; nor as it is a being in the genus of nature, even in the individual; but as it proceeds from a deficient created will; and therefore the moral malice, and the defect of sin, ought to be poured back upon the deficient will, and not upon God.
pass_b: The heading of chapter 9 reads: 'That God, by a prior motion, truly as an efficient cause or in the manner of a physical cause, premoves free choice to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being.'

The chapter opens: 'What has been said about the predetermination of the will to good acts must be extended to the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being. Hence whatever being is found in any act of sin, even one otherwise intrinsically evil, must be traced back to God as the first cause who premoves and, by an actual motion, predetermines the created will to that act insofar as it is an act and insofar as it is a being.'

Then, to show why it does not follow from God's being the first cause who premoves and predetermines the created will to an intrinsically evil act, such as blasphemy or hatred of God, that God causes the moral malice in such acts, he says this: the deformity of sin, or moral malice, does not follow intrinsically and by the nature of the case from the act of blasphemy or hatred of God in its essence as an act, nor as a being in the order of nature, even taken individually. It follows from the act as it comes from a created will that fails. The moral malice and the defect of sin must therefore be laid on the failing will, not on God.

lemmas.latin: in quantum actus, & ut ens est
lemmas.gloss: in so far as it is an act, and as it is a being

sections.title: Estius states the same and raises against himself the objection from freedom
sections.pass_a: And agreeable to these are the things which are read in Estius in the place cited above, where having set forth the same opinion, and adduced many things in its confirmation, he concludes thus, and objects to himself against the liberty of the human will, Since therefore it is plain from what has been said that our will is efficaciously moved and determined to its actions by God as the first cause, and first agent, mover, deliberator, and accordingly is prevented and predetermined by him, it remains to be explained how with that efficacious motion, and determination, nay divine premotion and predetermination, the liberty of our will consists. For that does not seem to be left free to either side which is efficaciously moved and determined by a prior cause to one part.
pass_b: What Estius writes in the passage cited above agrees with this. Having set out the same view and brought many arguments to support it, he concludes as follows and raises against himself the objection from the freedom of the human will:

'Since, then, what has been said makes it clear that our will is efficaciously moved and determined to its actions by God as first cause, first agent, mover and deliberator, and is therefore anticipated and predetermined by him, it remains to explain how the freedom of our will is consistent with that efficacious motion and determination, indeed with divine premotion and predetermination. For what a prior cause efficaciously moves and determines to one side does not seem to be left free to go either way.'

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

notes: 'deliberante' is printed as it stands in the 1675 text; it is not emended.

sections.title: Estius's answer: freedom requires choice from a judgment that could have been otherwise; only uncreated will has its choice from no prior
sections.pass_a: But to this he answers that for the nature of free choice; this suffices, that from a previous judgment of the practical intellect, it so choose one of opposites, that yet from a different judgment of the same intellect it could choose the other; because, namely, the root and foundation of liberty of choice is in the intellect, in so far as it can consider different reasons of good about opposites, and propose them to the will, but that the nature of free choice does not include, that while a free agent chooses from a previous judgment, it be not moved to so judging and choosing by some superior cause. And accordingly since the motion of God predetermining the will does not hinder that man have a full and perfect judgment of reason, and judge that one means is contingent, but another connected with the end by necessity, and that he could also choose another from a different judgment, by this very fact, such a motion does no harm to the liberty of our Will. Indeed it is proper to the uncreated Will that it does not have its choice from some prior.
pass_b: His answer is that for the nature of free choice it is enough that the will, on a prior judgment of the practical intellect, chooses one of two opposites in such a way that it could choose the other on a different judgment of the same intellect. The root and foundation of freedom of choice lies in the intellect, insofar as it can weigh different aspects of good in opposite options and set them before the will.

The nature of free choice does not require that a free agent, when it chooses on a prior judgment, should not be moved by some higher cause to judge and choose as it does. So, since God's motion predetermining the will does not prevent a man from having a full and complete judgment of reason, judging one means contingent and another necessarily connected with the end, and being able to choose differently on a different judgment, that motion does the freedom of our will no harm. It belongs only to the uncreated will not to receive its choice from something prior.

lemmas.gloss: the root and foundation of liberty

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Alvarez's other reconciliation: the premotion is needed to act actually, not to be able to act
sections.pass_a: Yet Alvarez endeavours by another reason to reconcile that Physical predetermination of the human Will to its several acts through the impulse of God moving, with the free choice of the same Will. For after he has proposed to himself this objection, if that previous influence of God into the cause is necessary, that the Will may operate, it follows that without it it cannot operate, and so its liberty will perish, He answers, That previous motion, or immediate influence into the cause, is not necessary that the Will can operate, if it will; for that it has through its proper Power, or through supernatural habits; but it is only necessary that it actually operate. Whence from this that the will is not moved by God by that previous motion, it does not follow that it cannot will, or operate; but it is only inferred that in fact it will not operate.
pass_b: Alvarez, however, tries another way to reconcile the physical predetermination of the human will to each of its acts by the impulse of God moving it with the will's free choice.

He sets himself this objection: 'If God's prior influence on the cause is necessary for the will to act, it follows that without it the will cannot act, and so its freedom is lost.' He replies: 'That prior motion, or immediate influence on the cause, is not needed for the will to be able to act if it wishes; it has that through its own power, or through supernatural habits. It is needed only for the will actually to act. So from the fact that God does not move the will by that prior motion, it does not follow that the will cannot will or act; it follows only that it will not in fact act.'

lemmas.gloss: in fact it will not operate

sections.title: Alvarez II.6: power to the contrary stands with predetermination in the divided sense; the omitter sins by his own fault
sections.pass_a: But in chap. 6 of the same book, in the Answer to the second argument, he denies that from this that God has predetermined someone to willing this, or that, it follows that absolutely speaking, it is not in his power to will something else, although from the supposition of that divine predetermination, it is impossible, in the composed sense, that he will another object. In a word he distinguishes between to will and to operate, and to be able to will and operate; and grants that without that predetermining influence the will never operates, but with it the will never fails to operate: but he contends, that with it the will has the power of not operating, and on the contrary without it the will has the power of operating, namely in the divided sense. Namely according to his mind, with that predetermining influence stands the potency of the will to not acting, or acting otherwise; but the opposite act does not stand, or cessation from the act. And vice versa, without that influence there remains in the will the potency of acting, although without it it is never brought out into act. But thence he gathers that it comes about that one omitting an act which is in precept omits it freely, and sins; because through sufficient help he could fulfil that precept; but from the mercy of God he could have that motion necessary for acting, but by his own fault he hindered that it should be given him by God.
pass_b: In chapter 6 of the same book, answering the second argument, he denies that because God has predetermined someone to will this or that, it is not, absolutely speaking, in his power to will something else, although on the supposition of that divine predetermination it is impossible, in the composite sense, for him to will another object.

In short, he distinguishes between willing and acting on the one hand and being able to will and act on the other. He grants that without that predetermining influence the will never acts, and that with it the will always acts. But he insists that with it the will has the power not to act, and without it the will has the power to act, in the divided sense. On his view the will's power not to act or to act otherwise coexists with the predetermining influence, but the opposite act, or ceasing from the act, does not. Conversely, without that influence the power to act remains in the will, though without it that power is never brought into act.

From this he concludes that someone who omits an act that is commanded omits it freely and sins. Through sufficient help he could have kept the command; by God's mercy he could have had the motion needed to act; and by his own fault he prevented God from giving it to him.

lemmas.latin: velle & operari, & posse velle atque operari
lemmas.gloss: to will and to operate, and to be able to will and operate

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Most Roman doctors now reject predetermination: it destroys freedom and makes God the author of sin
sections.pass_a: But by far the greater part of the Doctors of the Roman Church today rejects that opinion, and contends that that influence premoving and predetermining the wills of men to each of their acts, altogether overturns the liberty of human choice; and moreover that thence it follows that God is the author of sin, as one who, according to that opinion, predetermines men even to acts intrinsically evil, and imposes on them a certain necessity of acting ill.
pass_b: The great majority of the Roman Church's teachers, however, now reject this view. They argue that an influence premoving and predetermining human wills to each of their acts completely destroys the freedom of human choice.
They add that it would make God the author of sin, since on that view he predetermines people even to intrinsically evil acts and lays on them a kind of necessity to do wrong.

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.

sections.title: Their view: God concurs by acting on the action and effect, not on the faculty
sections.pass_a: Therefore they philosophize far otherwise about that concurrence of God. For first they lay down, that God concurring and cooperating with second causes does not do or imprint something on the faculty itself which acts, for example, on our will; but only immediately flows into and acts on the action itself, and the effect of the second cause, and produces it at that very moment at which it is produced by the second cause.
pass_b: They therefore reason about God's concurrence quite differently. First, they hold that when God concurs and cooperates with secondary causes he does not do or impress anything on the faculty that acts, our will, for instance.
He only flows into and acts directly on the action itself and on the effect of the secondary cause, producing it at the very moment the secondary cause produces it.

lemmas.gloss: flow into and act on the action itself

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: God's action is the creature's own action as receiving its being from God, not a distinct action on the will
sections.pass_a: Next consequently they teach that the action of the first cause concurring with the second cause, is not an action really different from the action of the second cause, but that very action, in so far as it receives its being from the first cause. So when God, for example, concurs with the will in the act of willing, or of refusing, he does not put forth, according to their mind, any action on the will, distinct from the action of the will itself; but only confers being on the action of the will together with the will, and preserves that action. And accordingly the divine cooperation in this part is not something different from our volition, but our volition itself, in so far as it depends immediately on God as to its production and preservation.
pass_b: Next, and consistently with this, they teach that the action of the first cause concurring with the secondary cause is not an action really distinct from that of the secondary cause. It is that same action, considered as receiving its being from the first cause.

So when God concurs with the will in an act of willing or refusing, he does not, on their view, exert on the will an action distinct from the will's own. He only gives being to the will's action together with the will, and keeps that action in being. God's cooperation here is therefore not something other than our act of will; it is our act of will itself, insofar as its production and preservation depend directly on God.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: So the secondary cause is not moved or determined by God; God's concurrence is indifferent and is determined by the creature
sections.pass_a: Moreover, which also manifestly follows from what has been said, they deny that the second cause is moved by the first cause to acting, or is determined by the same in acting to putting forth such an action. And so, according to their opinion, the second cause, and accordingly the will, does not operate because God moves it, and applies it to acting: but rather God cooperates with it, because it disposes itself to acting. But the divine concurrence and influence is something of itself indifferent, which is determined by second causes to the various species of actions.
pass_b: They also deny, as plainly follows from the foregoing, that the first cause moves the secondary cause to act or determines it, in acting, to produce a given action.

On their view, then, the secondary cause, and so the will, does not act because God moves it and applies it to act; rather, God cooperates with it because it sets itself to act. God's concurrence and influence is of itself indifferent, and it is the secondary causes that determine it to the various kinds of action.

lemmas.gloss: to the various species of actions

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.

sections.title: Molina's account in the Concordia (q. 14, disp. 26): one action, from God by general concurrence and from the creature by particular influence
sections.pass_a: These things and more of the same kind it is to be seen drawn out and set forth more at length in Luis Molina in the Concord of Free Choice with the gifts of grace, &c. quest. 14. disput. 26. Where he affirms first that God so concurs with second causes to their operations and effects, that as the second cause immediately elicits its operation, and through it produces the term, or effect; so God by a certain general concurrence immediately flows with it into the same operation, and through the operation, or action produces its term, or effect. Secondly, that God, when he concurs with second causes, flows in as a universal cause, by a certain influence indifferent to various actions and effects, but that that general influence is determined to diverse species of actions and effects by the particular influence of second causes, which is diverse according to the diversity of the power of each to acting. Not otherwise than the influence of the sun, which also is universal, is determined by the influence of man, that a man be produced; and by the influence of a horse, that a horse arise. But if the cause be free, it is in its power so to flow in, that this action rather than that be produced, say to will, rather than to refuse, or to walk, rather than to sit, and this effect rather than that, namely this artefact, rather than another; Or also to suspend the influence altogether, that there be no action. Thirdly, that for the production of no effect is the influence of God through universal concurrence sufficient, without the influence of the particular second cause by which it is determined, nor in turn the influence of the particular cause, without the influence of God through universal concurrence, by which it is helped, and which he has decreed by ordinary law never to deny. But that these two influences depend mutually on each other, that they may exist in the nature of things: nay that they are not two actions, but one action in number, which as it is from God flowing in that manner, is called general concurrence; but as from the second cause, say from fire heating, is called the concurrence, or influence of fire. Nor does that action have that it is of this species, namely heating, rather than cooling, because it is from God through universal concurrence, but because it is from the fire with God cooperating through its particular power.
pass_b: These points, and more of the same kind, are worked out and explained at greater length by Luis de Molina in his Concordia of free choice with the gifts of grace, question 14, disputation 26.

He states, first, that God concurs with secondary causes in their operations and effects in this way: just as the secondary cause directly produces its operation and through it brings about its result or effect, so God, by a general concurrence, flows directly together with it into that same operation and through the operation or action brings about its result or effect.

Second, when God concurs with secondary causes he acts as a universal cause, by an influence indifferent to various actions and effects, and that general influence is determined to different kinds of action and effect by the particular influence of secondary causes, which differs according to the different power each has to act. The sun's influence, which is likewise universal, is determined by a man's influence to produce a man and by a horse's influence to produce a horse. If the cause is free, it is in its power to exert its influence so that this action rather than that results, say willing rather than refusing, or walking rather than sitting, and this effect rather than that, this artefact rather than another. Or it can withhold its influence altogether, so that there is no action at all.

Third, God's influence through universal concurrence is not enough to produce any effect without the influence of the particular secondary cause that determines it. Nor, conversely, is the particular cause's influence enough without God's influence through universal concurrence, which helps it and which by ordinary law God has resolved never to withhold. These two influences depend on each other in order to exist in reality; indeed they are not two actions but numerically one action. As it comes from God acting in that way it is called general concurrence; as it comes from the secondary cause, say from fire heating something, it is called the concurrence or influence of the fire. And that action is of this kind, heating rather than cooling, not because it comes from God through universal concurrence but because it comes from the fire, with God cooperating, through the fire's particular power.
